question: Will the UK increase the qualifying period for settlement to 10 years before May 2026?
summary: There is a strong official policy trajectory toward raising the default settlement qualifying period to 10 years (Earned Settlement), with exemptions for certain categories.
Public briefings and consultations indicate rollout could begin around April 2026, aiming for the new threshold to be in effect for new applicants by May 2026.
Exemption and category-specific rules temper universality, meaning not all routes would see a full 10-year wait.
Credible risks exist (legislative passage, operational readiness) that could delay or temper the rollout, though the near-term direction remains toward a 10-year baseline.

justification.critique_assessment: Objections are valid and describe real risks (legislation, implementation readiness, exemptions), but they do not overturn the near-term trajectory suggested by official materials.
justification.adjustment: No adjustment; final probability remains the ensemble aggregate (0.97) as the threshold analysis indicates a high likelihood of the 10-year baseline being in force for new applicants by May 2026, albeit with exemptions and transitional rules.

forecasts.reference-class: UK immigration policy changes to settlement thresholds (earned settlement) proposing a baseline 10-year qualifying period for Indefinite Leave to Remain, with exceptions by category and potential faster routes for high earners or specific visa holders.

sources.claim: The default qualifying period for settlement will be increased from the current 5 years to 10 years, with exceptions.
The government announced more details on 20 November 2025 that the baseline qualifying period for many migrants would be ten years.
Migration Observatory explains a 10-year baseline for settlement with exceptions and longer periods for some groups.
Home Office consultation indicates the standard ILR qualifying period will rise to 10 years, with 15 years for lower-skilled workers; implementation planned (April 2026).
The Guardian reports the government proposing to extend waiting period for permanent settlement from five to ten years.
GOV.UK states that earned settlement will increase the standard qualifying period for settlement to ten years, with potential reductions based on contributions to the economy and society.
House of Commons Library explains the baseline qualifying period would be ten years for many migrants, with exceptions and durations dependent on individual circumstances.
GOV.UK notes that the long residence rule requires at least 10 years continuous lawful presence in the UK before qualification for settlement.
A law-firm analysis cites the consultation closing February 12, 2026 and potential implementation as early as April 2026.

Migration Observatory commentary emphasizes that the reforms center on a 10-year baseline with longer or shorter waits depending on various factors, and that many migrants would face longer or equal waiting periods.

House of Commons Library briefing confirms the government announced details on 20 November 2025 that the baseline period would be 10 years with exceptions, with rollout potentially starting in April 2026.
GOV.UK consultation document states the default qualifying period will increase to 10 years within an earned settlement model, with a four-pillar framework.
Littler summarizes the government’s open consultation (launched Nov 2025) proposing a 10-year baseline and phased implementation.
Migration Observatory commentary outlines the 10-year baseline with exceptions and notes the potential impact on different immigration routes.
Guardian reports the white paper proposals would extend waiting time for settlement, potentially affecting about 1.5 million migrants.
FT analysis discusses risk to non-working partners and the broader implications of the reforms to settlement timelines.
